qAndA.answer: While the colors change over time and for each nanoparticle pair, in the initial slides green represents crystalline structures while orange represents amorphous structures.
qAndA.question: What is the color coding used for the atoms in the 3D models?

qAndA.answer: The MSD graph shows a steeper slope for surface atoms compared to core atoms, indicating that surface atoms move significantly more over time, supporting the idea of localized surface diffusion.
qAndA.question: How does the MSD graph support the observation of localized surface diffusion?

qAndA.answer: It challenges the commonly held assumption that surface atoms in nanoparticles are highly mobile and contribute to diffusion across the entire surface. This finding suggests a more nuanced understanding of surface diffusion mechanisms in core-shell nanoparticles.
qAndA.question: Why is the finding of localized surface diffusion considered significant?

qAndA.answer: The video consistently shows two nanoparticles coalescing for each simulation, suggesting only a single pair was simulated for each type of nanoparticle.
qAndA.question: How many nanoparticle pairs were simulated for each type?

qAndA.answer: The video maintains a neutral and informative mood throughout, focusing on presenting scientific findings and their implications. It sparks curiosity with the unexpected observation of localized surface diffusion but remains grounded in objective data analysis.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hello, my name is Namsoon, I'm a postdoc from Lund University in Sweden. My poster is about
the centering mechanism of causal nanoparticles. Centering of nanoparticle is important because
how the shape and the structure of nanoparticle change due to centering has huge impact on the
performance of the functional nanoparticles in given applications. Centering mechanisms of
pure crystalline metal nanoparticles had been investigated previously, but there was no study on
particles that have crystalline metal core with amorphous metal oxide shell. And because these metal
metal oxide core shell system itself is gathering much attention as a functional nanoparticle,
we studied their centering behavior by using molecular dynamics. So we prepared three different types
of metal, metal oxide, causal nanoparticles, which exhibit crystalline core and amorphous metal
oxide shell after equilibrium at given temperatures. Then we let the nanoparticles merge and coalesce
together and studied how the atoms diffuse during the centering process. Here it shows how to
nickel oxide core and nanoparticles coalesce over a period of time. And for the other two types of
nanoparticles as well. A common feature we observed in all three types of nanoparticles is that
the core atoms do not diffuse across the boundary zone between the two clusters, and the surface
atoms do not diffuse onto the other side of the nanoparticle surface either. But of course if we
plot and compare the mean square displacement, MST of surface atoms and core atoms, we can see that
the surface atoms are the one diffuse more and therefore contribute to the centering processes.
So in that sense, the mechanism here was similar to that of the pure crystalline metal nanoparticles.
One thing that was quite interesting was that when we traced the atomic trajectory,
we could see that the diffusion was highly localized. What we mean by that is, as we can see here,
for example, we are tracing the atoms that are far away from the contact region, and we can see
that the atoms remain pretty much where they were while the centering progress is quite significantly.
And this is quite contrasting to the commonly known concept of the high mobility of
liquid-like surface atoms and surface diffusion of nanoparticles.
Thank you for watching and for more detailed information, please read my poster.
